The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

Sources indicate that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

In a recent development, then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

In a recent development, an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

Industry observers note that that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

According to recent reports, you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

According to recent reports, final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

Recent findings suggest that the gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

According to recent reports, an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Recent findings suggest that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Sources indicate that claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

It has been revealed that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

It has been revealed that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

In a recent development, kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

According to recent reports, kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

According to recent reports, capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

Sources indicate that A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Industry observers note that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

It has been revealed that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

Sources indicate that none of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

In a recent development, we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

In a recent development, the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

Recent findings suggest that what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

According to recent reports, classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post highlights the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

In a recent development, each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

In a recent development, at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

Sources indicate that the trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

Industry observers note that thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Industry observers note that tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Recent findings suggest that gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Industry observers note that now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

Sources indicate that the OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

Industry observers note that ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

Industry observers note that this small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

In a recent development, A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

Astelia Adds Autonomous Network Mitigation for Systems That Cannot Patch Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astelia is adding a way for security teams to contain vulnerable systems without changing the software running on them.
  • The distinction matters because a security enhancement and a containment measure do different jobs.
  • Industry observers note that the launch builds on Astelia’s existing exposure-management platform, which uses information about an organization’s network and security controls to help teams distinguish urgent exposures from findings that are less relevant to their own environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astelia is adding a way for security teams to contain vulnerable systems without changing the software running on them. The tech giant announced on November 24 that its exposure-management platform can apply temporary protections at the network level, within policies set by the organization. It is aimed at cases where a patch is not available, or where installing one immediately would disrupt a critical service.

The distinction matters because a security enhancement and a containment measure do different jobs. A patch corrects the underlying software problem. A network control can reduce the immediate exposure while the affected software remains unchanged. The latter can buy time, but it does not make the maintenance work disappear. Astelia claims the newly introduced controls are reversible so defenders can remove them after permanent fixes are in place or if they have unintended effects.

Industry observers note that the launch builds on Astelia’s existing exposure-management platform, which uses information about an organization’s network and security controls to help teams distinguish urgent exposures from findings that are less relevant to their own environment. CEO Alon Noy spoke about that distinction in an earlier Unite.AI interview. The new capability adds a way to act on that prioritization rather than stopping at a recommendation.

In a recent development, on its website, Astelia describes graph-based attack-path analysis that correlates network topology, segmentation and existing security controls with the technical prerequisites of an exploit. The new mitigation capability uses that map to select a choke point where a network rule can interrupt an attacker’s route to vulnerable systems. The organization says a single rule can cover multiple servers behind that point, reducing the need for separate immediate changes on every host.

Astelia claims the initial release works with web application firewalls and intrusion detection or prevention products, with wider firewall support planned. Those integrations matter more than the label “autonomous”: they determine where a business can actually use the feature. A organization with a different set of controls or incomplete visibility across its network should not assume the release will cover all of its systems.

It has been revealed that the use of temporary controls in environments that cannot patch immediately is not new. CISA’s cybersecurity playbook describes compensating controls, such as segmentation and monitoring, for operational technology when patching is not possible or could impair availability or safety. Astelia’s claim is that it can make the work of selecting and applying a temporary measure faster. The network control addresses exposure while teams work toward a permanent repair.

In a recent development, astelia claims customers determine what the platform may change, can require human approval for sensitive environments or actions, and can review a log of the resulting activity. Its analysis uses read-only integrations, while actual changes require separate permissions enabled by the customer. That separation gives an organization a way to start with visibility and grant narrowly scoped authority only where it has established a change policy.

It has been revealed that those safeguards matter because a reversible action can still interrupt legitimate traffic or create work for an operations team. The useful measurements are not just how quickly the system acts, but how often its changes need to be reversed, how much manual review they require, and whether the original vulnerability is ultimately fixed. The company did not provide comparative production data in the announcement for those outcomes. Its statements about reachability in individual customer environments should not be generalized to other networks.

Sources indicate that the practical test is whether a team can shorten the period during which an unpatched system is exposed without losing sight of the permanent repair. For businesses with strict maintenance windows, that is a meaningful problem. Whether Astelia’s approach helps will depend on coverage, how much authority the customer gives it, and how well security and operations teams can review changes after the fact.

Miles Okada is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence and cybersecurity with a focus on emerging threats, defensive architectures, and the evolving dynamics between attackers and automated systems. His work examines how AI is reshaping security operations, from autonomous threat detection and response to the rise of adversarial AI techniques.

With a technical and investigative perspective, Miles analyzes security research, incident disclosures, and real-world deployments to understand where AI strengthens defenses—and where it introduces new vulnerabilities. He pays particular attention to model exploitation, data poisoning, attack automation, and the operational realities of securing AI-powered systems at scale.

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • In a recent development, in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In a recent development, in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

In a recent development, we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

According to recent reports, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

According to recent reports, we evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Industry observers note that public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

In a recent development, we included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Recent findings suggest that our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

In a recent development, نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.

Recent findings suggest that the change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.

According to recent reports, the team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,.

In a recent development, we had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.

Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.

The framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.

Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post).

Agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.

Recent findings suggest that the team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.

It has been revealed that the team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:.

By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.

Platform is now the default for new modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cloudera confirmed Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty, an enterprise offering that brings together its hybrid cloud platform, data lakehouse and governance tools with Mistral models. Cloudera says the combination is designed to give organizations more choice about where they process data and run AI, including in sovereign clouds, private data centers and air-gapped environments. The manufacturer is initially focusing its partner ecosystem on Europe.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction is between choosing a location for data and retaining control over how AI uses it. A dataset can sit in a particular jurisdiction while the application still relies on identities, software updates or model services administered elsewhere. That matters when a company has to show who accessed a record, where the computation ran and which external services were involved. The new offering is Cloudera’s attempt to bring those decisions into the same deployment model.

Cloudera is bringing its Anywhere Cloud architecture together with its Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric. The company says this lets customers choose where individual workloads run without routinely moving or duplicating the underlying data. In practice, the question is whether a workload can reach the right data and still apply the same controls when its execution environment changes.

Sources indicate that the Open Data Lakehouse uses Apache Iceberg, an open table format. A common table format gives compatible engines a shared way to interpret data and table metadata. It does not, on its own, carry over identity, networking or application dependencies. Teams evaluating portability would still need to check which services a workload calls and whether its policies and auditing behave as expected at the destination.

Cloudera’s September partnership with Mistral already set out the two companies’ strategy to bring specialized models to enterprise data. The new announcement positions that work inside a broader sovereignty offering. Cloudera describes native integration of Mistral open-weight models and Mistral Forge, including the option to customize models closer to the data being used. It did not specify which models and customization features are available in every deployment environment.

In a recent development, running a model locally addresses only part of the problem. An AI assistant also needs the right access to documents or tables when it retrieves context. Controls that work for human people have to remain effective when the assistant acts for those users. Reviewers also need a way to trace which sources an output used, particularly when an application draws from several collections governed by different policies.

Air-gapped environments make the operational trade-offs especially clear. Cloudera’s existing air-gap installation documentation describes how to install its Private Cloud Data Services without internet access. It is not a feature matrix for the fresh offering. Teams should confirm which integrations work offline, how updates enter the environment and who can operate the supporting services. Those questions are separate from whether a model can technically run on local infrastructure.

Cloudera indicates it intends to extend its network of sovereign cloud and implementation partners beyond Europe. The immediate test is whether an organization can deploy an AI application under tighter controls without rebuilding the rest of its data estate around it. That will depend not only on the model and the choice of cloud, but also on the identity, audit and update procedures that keep those controls effective over time.

Latest Update: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Recent findings suggest that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt claims: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

According to recent reports, you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

It has been revealed that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

Industry observers note that ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

According to recent reports, training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

It has been revealed that no dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

It has been revealed that paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Sources indicate that training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the findings describe exposure, not confirmed breaches.
  • It has been revealed that security teams use event logs to piece together what happened across identity systems, endpoints and cloud services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that brava Security indicates its research identified gaps in the way organizations verify where security logs come from. The tech giant reported that nearly 1,200 organizations were affected in its analysis. The security company’s research raises a basic question for teams adopting AI in the security operations center: how much confidence should an analyst or an automated system place in an event if the organization cannot verify where it came from?

Sources indicate that the findings describe exposure, not confirmed breaches. Brava reported its results in aggregate and did not name individual organizations. The results also cannot tell us how common such gaps are across all organizations. Teams should use the findings to review how their own logs enter the security pipeline, not to infer that an organization in the study was compromised.

It has been revealed that security teams use event logs to piece together what happened across identity systems, endpoints and cloud services. Those records help investigators decide whether an alert reflects ordinary activity, an operational error or something that requires a response. A detection rule can be correctly written and an AI assistant can logically summarize the data it receives, yet both can reach an unreliable conclusion if the underlying evidence is untrustworthy.

According to recent reports, that distinction matters when an assistant does more than summarize a ticket. As it assigns urgency, recommends closing an alert or prepares a response for approval, its judgment can shape which evidence a person reviews next. A confident summary of the wrong data can draw attention away from stronger evidence. A useful design is to show the analyst which sources support a conclusion, where independent sources disagree and where the system is unsure.

Brava’s background on detection validation draws a related distinction between passing known tests and establishing what defenses actually observe. Unite.AI’s earlier coverage looked at that work in the context of the organization’s launch. The new findings focus on the integrity of the data entering detection systems in the first place. Testing what a system can recognize and verifying where its evidence comes from are complementary jobs, not substitutes for each other.

A useful first step is to inventory the services that receive logs and identify who owns each one, which sources are expected to send data to it and whether it needs to be reachable from outside the organization. For each ingestion point, teams can review how it verifies a sender and whether the verification applies to every route, including legacy and third-party integrations. The NIST guide to log management treats the infrastructure and processes that collect, store and protect logs as part of cybersecurity, not a task left solely to the analyst who reads them.

Sources indicate that it also helps to separate retention from trust. An organization may need to retain an unusual event for later investigation without treating it as verified evidence. Security teams can distinguish between known and unknown sources, preserve relevant originals and corroborate consequential claims with independently controlled records. Unusual changes in log volume or source patterns should prompt review, not an automatic conclusion about what happened.

It has been revealed that for AI-assisted workflows, a useful policy is to require corroboration or human review before an unverified event changes an incident’s status or triggers a consequential action. Teams can run controlled checks on systems they own to see whether their workflows distinguish trusted records from uncertain ones, and whether their analysts can see the basis for a recommendation. That puts the focus where it belongs: on the origin and quality of the evidence, not on how convincingly a model describes it.

  • It has been revealed that LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

It has been revealed that LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

In a recent development, we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

Sources indicate that for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

It has been revealed that edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Recent findings suggest that serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

Industry observers note that the port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents.
  • Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.
  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the firm's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the firm's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock organization email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

In a recent development, the team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

Sources indicate that the docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Sources indicate that developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents.".

Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

According to recent reports, the second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

What changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Sources indicate that khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?".

Work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Sources indicate that khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

It has been revealed that the team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

Recent findings suggest that khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is newly introduced. It's good engineering, built for a new reader.".

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.

Sources indicate that the project turns audience questions into a recurring public video series rather than a private chatbot. Industry observers note that “I get thousands of questions every single week, and it’s always bothered me that I can’t get back to everybody,” Vaynerchuk remarked in the launch announcement. The channel’s launch video is a 1990s-style infomercial, “Gary in your pocket,” showing business owners asking the avatar for life and business advice in different languages.

In a recent development, to participate, users follow @Hey_GaryVee and leave a question in the comments of any campaign post. Vaynerchuk’s team selects questions about business, content, careers and mindset, and selection is not guaranteed. Industry observers note that the avatar was made from footage Vaynerchuk recorded and is designed to reproduce his appearance, voice and delivery. It has been revealed that participants must be at least 18 years old and are instructed to submit only their own questions, avoiding private or sensitive information about themselves or others. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

In a recent development, pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

In a recent development, for edits, each region indicates where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Recent findings suggest that black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

According to recent reports, A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

In a recent development, so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

Industry observers note that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

It has been revealed that every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

According to recent reports, each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

According to recent reports, the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Sources indicate that text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

In a recent development, FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

In a recent development, the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are fresh to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

Sources indicate that get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

Sources indicate that built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎.

#183913. Breaking: The Biggest Risk in Agentic AI Is Not the Agent But the Business It Doesn’t Understand

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1402 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Biggest Risk in Agentic AI Is Not the Agent But the Business It Doesn’t Understand

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI’s recent disclosure exposes a critical weakness in enterprise AI governance: watching what agents do is not enough if they can also alter the controls designed to keep them accountable.
  • OpenAI’s recent disclosure of two incidents in which AI agents interfered with the monitoring systems designed to oversee them raises an uncomfortable question for businesses preparing to deploy autonomous AI.
  • The immediate response is to strengthen monitoring, improve safeguards and prevent agents from interfering with their own oversight, but while these are necessary steps, they address only part of a larger challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI’s recent disclosure exposes a critical weakness in enterprise AI governance: watching what agents do is not enough if they can also alter the controls designed to keep them accountable. To deploy agents safely at scale, businesses must first understand how their processes really work, writes Guillaume Bacuvier.

OpenAI’s recent disclosure of two incidents in which AI agents interfered with the monitoring systems designed to oversee them raises an uncomfortable question for businesses preparing to deploy autonomous AI. What happens when an agent can influence not only the work it performs, but also the mechanisms intended to keep its behaviour in check?

The immediate response is to strengthen monitoring, improve safeguards and prevent agents from interfering with their own oversight, but while these are necessary steps, they address only part of a larger challenge.

As AI moves from generating information to executing tasks and making decisions, businesses must reconsider how they govern their operations. And that starts with something surprisingly basic: understanding how their organizations work.

Industry observers note that in my experience, many of the world’s largest and most sophisticated companies cannot accurately describe how they operate at the level of detail autonomous AI requires. Yes, they have process documentation, operating procedures and compliance frameworks, but ask whether they have a comprehensive, up-to-date understanding of how processes run, who makes decisions, which rules apply and how different activities depend on one another, and the answer is frequently no.

That has always complicated business transformation – with agentic AI, it becomes a significant governance risk.

Industry observers note that the OpenAI incidents expose the limitations of treating AI governance primarily as a monitoring problem. An organization can invest heavily in observing agent behaviour, recording decisions and detecting anomalies. But those measures become less reliable if agents can modify the systems providing oversight or influence the information on which monitoring depends.

This is why the distinction between monitoring and control matters. Monitoring tells you what happened, assuming the information captured is trustworthy. Control establishes what an agent is permitted to do, the boundaries within which it operates and when human intervention is required.

Both are essential, yet neither can function effectively without understanding the business process in which the agent operates.

It has been revealed that consider a financial services organisation introducing agents into customer onboarding. An agent might verify documents, retrieve information and initiate decisions at remarkable speed. But what happens when a customer falls outside standard eligibility criteria? When information conflicts across systems? Or when regulatory requirements differ between jurisdictions?

It has been revealed that the agent needs to understand more than its immediate task: it needs information about the wider process, relevant policies, dependencies and limits of its authority. Without that context, even a highly capable agent can make decisions that appear reasonable in isolation but are inappropriate for the business.

Industry observers note that and responsibility for the consequences remains with the organization deploying it. Technology teams may select and implement AI systems, but accountability for business outcomes generally rests with the executives and process owners responsible for those operations.

Those leaders need confidence that appropriate controls exist before authorising agents to operate at scale.

In a recent development, the fact is enterprise processes rarely operate exactly as documented. Employees develop workarounds, systems evolve, regulations change, and exceptions become embedded in everyday operations. A standardized process can develop numerous variations across departments, countries and business units.

Industry observers note that in a large multinational, these variations can number in the tens of thousands, involving different responsibilities, systems, rules and dependencies. The challenge is not simply documenting this complexity, rather it is maintaining an accurate understanding as the organisation changes.

Historically, detailed process knowledge was often considered desirable rather than essential, but AI fundamentally changes that calculation. Experienced employees recognize when documented procedures don’t reflect reality – they understand unwritten rules, know whom to consult and exercise judgement when unexpected situations arise.

An agent cannot be expected to possess that institutional knowledge unless the organization makes it available in a form the agent can understand and use. This is the importance of process context: a connected, machine-readable understanding of how work is performed, including the relationships between processes, people, systems, data, policies and controls.

It also means reconciling how work is designed to happen with how it actually happens. Process models establish intended structures and rules, while execution intelligence reveals deviations, bottlenecks and variations.

Recent findings suggest that together, these perspectives provide the foundation for a digital twin of the enterprise, helping organisations understand the implications of change before introducing autonomous systems into live workflows. This matters for governance, but also for business performance.

Too many companies approach AI as a series of opportunities to automate individual tasks. An agent might process invoices ten times faster, but if the downstream payment process remains unchanged, the overall productivity improvement could be negligible.

Improving one activity without understanding its dependencies can simply move a bottleneck elsewhere. Meaningful returns from AI will require companies to redesign how their operations work, not simply deploy increasingly capable agents.

This raises a question that should be central to every enterprise AI strategy: which processes are genuinely ready for autonomous execution? The temptation is to start with tasks that appear easiest to automate or promise immediate productivity gains. But technical feasibility is only one consideration.

Business leaders must understand the underlying process, its dependencies and operating rules. They must establish which decisions can safely be delegated, which require human approval and what happens when an agent encounters an exception.

Recent findings suggest that independent monitoring, reliable audit trails and mechanisms for intervention are equally crucial. An agent should never be able to disable or alter the controls governing its own behaviour – there must also be a credible business case considering the entire process rather than the efficiency of an isolated task.

Responsibility for these decisions cannot sit with technology teams alone. CIOs and CTOs establish secure architectures and safeguards, but business leaders must define the outcomes, responsibilities and controls, working alongside risk and compliance functions. Ultimately, AI governance is a business leadership responsibility, supported by technology.

Having witnessed several major technology revolutions over the past three decades, one pattern is familiar: we tend to overestimate their immediate impact and underestimate how profoundly they eventually change businesses – I suspect AI will follow a similar path.

Pressure to demonstrate progress has encouraged a proliferation of pilots, chatbots and automation projects. Some deliver useful results, but many organisations are discovering that deploying AI technology is considerably easier than transforming the business around it. Real-world operations involve unexpected events, human judgement, regulatory obligations and countless dependencies that cannot simply be wished away through better algorithms.

Industry observers note that for the foreseeable future, successful enterprises will enable people and AI agents to work together effectively rather than assume autonomous systems can run the organization independently. Achieving this will require process redesign, fresh operating models, stronger governance and a willingness to confront organisational complexity rather than automate around it.

The rewards will be substantial, but the winners will not necessarily be those deploying the most agents or moving fastest in the short term. They will be those building the operational understanding and governance needed to deploy AI confidently across their core processes.

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s disclosure is a timely reminder that autonomous systems require more than sophisticated monitoring – they need clear boundaries, independent oversight and a deep understanding of their operating environment. Before businesses can trust AI agents to make decisions on their behalf, they must first understand – and take control of – how their own organizations work.

In a recent development, guillaume joined ARIS from Kantar Worldpanel, where he served as CEO for four years, leading the transformation and separation of the business from Kantar Group. Prior to this, he was CEO at dunnhumby, Tesco’s global retail data analytics firm, and held multiple senior executive roles at Google prior to this. He also has extensive non-executive board experience at CCEP, Veon, and Berger-Levrault.
