#183910. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3035 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Recent findings suggest that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Recent findings suggest that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post reveals you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Recent findings suggest that meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that looks, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the latest modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

In a recent development, the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

In a recent development, only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

It has been revealed that the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

It has been revealed that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

Industry observers note that as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

Sources indicate that the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

Recent findings suggest that <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server.

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:.

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:.

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

Sources indicate that llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:.

Sources indicate that the checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:.

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:.

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

In a recent development, we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning indicates up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Industry observers note that note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

Recent findings suggest that the language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

This is a major model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/fresh/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section indicates how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Sources indicate that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

In a recent development, we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

According to recent reports, we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

In a recent development, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

In a recent development, hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

According to recent reports, you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Applied Systems unveiled on November 24, 2026 that it had acquired Tailwind, an insurance document and data retrieval specialist, to move carrier documents automatically into its management systems and expand AI automation across agencies’ operational, financial and trading workflows.

Recent findings suggest that the acquisition addresses the gap between documents held by carriers and the data agencies need inside their management systems. Applied CEO Graham Blackwell said: “Critical insurance workflows depend on risk and policy data, yet that data is locked in documents behind carrier portals and across fragmented systems.” Tailwind adds retrieval and normalization technology for moving that information into Applied’s software.

According to recent reports, applied expects the combination to reduce back-office costs and support growth by extending automation across the risk lifecycle. The practical significance is a shared intake path for information that would otherwise require agency staff to search portals, monitor email and move documents between systems.

According to recent reports, tailwind’s software collects insurance documents, standardizes their data and produces client reports used when pursuing new accounts and renewing existing ones. Tailwind reports in its product documentation that it retrieves loss runs—carrier records of claims histories—from more than 1,000 carriers, wholesalers and managing general agents through portals, email and direct connections.

Sources indicate that agencies can schedule retrieval before a renewal, while Tailwind manages carrier contact, follow-up, authorization paperwork and broker-of-record letters. Request statuses show which documents have arrived and which still need attention.

In a recent development, tailwind’s AI reads claims from the varied formats used for loss runs and standardizes paid, reserved and incurred values so policy years and carriers can be compared without re-keying the data. A separate mailroom capability consolidates documents arriving by carrier email, portal download or upload. It classifies items such as policies, quotes, endorsements and loss runs, then associates each with the correct client, policy and term in the agency management system.

Recent findings suggest that once standardized, the claims data can be turned into agency-branded summaries and analyses of frequency, severity, loss causes, large claims and open reserves. For a brokerage, one intake process can therefore feed both a fresh-business submission and the claims discussion at renewal, with the original loss runs available alongside a multi-year claims history for underwriters.

Recent findings suggest that applied prepares to use Tailwind across the three domains of Epic Conductor, the AI platform built into Applied Epic that it launched on September 29, 2026. Those domains are operational automation, financial automation and connected trading. Epic Conductor already includes AI extraction from carrier documents, automated reconciliation with human review and submission workflows linking agencies and carriers; Tailwind is intended to extend the documents and data available to those processes.

For financial automation, Applied intends to retrieve employee-benefits commission statements and property-and-casualty statements that are not delivered by download. The initiative is to remove the monthly step in which agencies locate and upload those statements before automated reconciliation, connecting document retrieval directly to the accounting workflow.

It has been revealed that applied also wants information from non-downloaded policies and client messages to fill the appropriate agency-management fields automatically for work such as starting a submission or setting up a plan record. For connected trading, loss-run data retrieved from carriers would populate renewal and new-business submissions. All three remain planned Epic Conductor integrations.

Applied’s acquisition FAQ notes the majority of Tailwind’s customers already use Applied Epic, and that Tailwind customers and partners will see no change to their primary services or support contacts following the acquisition.

That overlap makes deeper Epic integration immediately relevant to much of Tailwind’s installed base. The continuity commitment is also consequential because Tailwind’s software handles documents used in time-sensitive renewal and submission work.

It has been revealed that for Applied, the deal is intended to turn document access into a shared input for agency operations, commission reconciliation and carrier submissions. The central execution question is whether the planned Epic Conductor connections can remove portal searches, monthly statement uploads and claims re-keying across whole workflows, rather than merely speeding individual retrieval tasks.

He is particularly interested in how insurers balance automation with accountability in high-stakes decision-making systems.

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j.

Nov 23, 2026 7 min read.

This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

Industry observers note that oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Revision Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

In a recent development, JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

Industry observers note that JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.

Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various complications. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

A upcoming Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:.

[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

According to recent reports, organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:.

Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a fresh block of IDs.

Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

According to recent reports, the release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Upgrade (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

Industry observers note that the release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

Sources indicate that the formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.

Industry observers note that after two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and fresh features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All latest data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

It has been revealed that we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Recent findings suggest that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

According to recent reports, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Sources indicate that access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team unveiled the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Recent findings suggest that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

According to recent reports, if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

Industry observers note that A launch can have an active team channel and still miss its deadline. The conversations are happening, but nobody has a reliable view of ownership, overdue work, and dependencies. Slack and monday.com address different parts of that problem: Slack brings people and connected tools into the conversation, while monday.com turns work into records that managers can organize and monitor.

In a recent development, choose Slack when coordination, fast answers, and bringing colleagues into the same discussion are the immediate problem. Choose monday.com when you need a shared operational blueprint with clear owners, dates, views, and reporting. For a growing team with both needs, we favor using Slack as the communication layer and monday.com as the delivery record.

Sources indicate that both products appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide. This comparison evaluates where each belongs in a real team workflow, including where using them together is more useful than replacing one with the other.

Sources indicate that A ten-person services team is onboarding three customers at once. Every customer needs a kickoff, document collection, setup work, and approval before launch. The team needs to answer two different questions: what needs a conversation today, and which deliverables are at risk?

In Slack, give each customer engagement a channel and keep the scope, key links, and decision owners in a canvas. A list can hold the deliverables, assignees, and due dates. Discussion stays close to the work because individual list items have their own threads. That is a useful starting point for a team whose current alternative is chasing direct messages.

In monday.com, represent each engagement on a board with a named owner, a due date, and a status. A manager can compare the three engagements without opening every conversation. Timeline and Gantt views on the appropriate paid plan make the sequence of deliverables easier to understand. The team can still discuss an item, but the structured board remains the place to answer whether it is ready.

Recent findings suggest that our preference shifts toward monday.com when the same team starts handling ten or twenty concurrent engagements. Repeated reporting, cross-board visibility, and dependencies become more valuable than the convenience of keeping every action in chat. Slack remains valuable for resolving the exceptions: a missing approval, a newly discovered requirement, or a customer question that needs several people.

In Slack, a useful AI request starts with work the team has already discussed: summarize the open questions, explain a decision, or prepare a brief for someone joining the project. Slackbot’s value comes from the relevant context it can access, not from replacing an accountable owner. The official example below shows research being organized into a canvas; it is a vendor product example, not a result from our own test.

In a recent development, monday.com’s AI works naturally on board information. For example, a team can use a field-based prompt to summarize a customer request or classify an incoming item, then review the result in the same operational view. Sidekick adds conversational assistance around the work. The notable difference is the output: a usable field or board action is more directly connected to the process than another paragraph in a channel.

Sources indicate that for the onboarding example, we would use Slack to prepare a short brief from the customer discussion and monday.com to keep the resulting delivery commitments organized. A summary saying the team agreed to launch Friday does not replace a due date and owner. Conversely, a red status cell does not explain the customer’s concern as well as the underlying conversation.

Plan choice matters for this workflow. Slack Free and Pro provide a limited Slackbot preview; Business+ includes 15 messages per member each week, with additional usage available through the applicable credit arrangement. Permission and connected-app scope determine what the assistant can use. A paid communication plan and unrestricted AI usage are different purchases.

In a recent development, slack’s official overview below demonstrates how AI fits into the communication workspace. Use it to understand the product’s approach alongside the concrete work examples above.

Recent findings suggest that slack AI | AI that works where you do. Video: Slack.

The monday.com overview provides a second view of the decision: how a team organizes its work in a shared operational workspace.

Recent findings suggest that monday.com Work OS | Your best work, your way. Video: monday.com.

According to recent reports, the monday.com Slack integration can send board updates into channels and create items from Slack conversations. Start with one customer board and one channel, then send only events that require attention, such as blocked work or an approval request. Announcing every edit recreates the noise the integration was supposed to remove.

Keep monday.com responsible for status and Slack responsible for the discussion about it. When someone resolves a blocker in Slack, revision the board rather than relying on readers to infer that the work is complete. App approval, the connected account, and regional feature availability still affect the setup; monday.com documents limitations for some Slack features on EU-hosted accounts.

Recent findings suggest that the examples below use standard USD annual-billing rates, expressed as a monthly equivalent. They exclude tax, temporary promotions, and additional AI usage. Annual billing means paying the annual commitment, rather than buying a month at the displayed equivalent.

Recent findings suggest that for a ten-person team, Slack Pro plus monday.com Standard is a $192.50 monthly equivalent, or $2,310 billed annually, using the standard USD annual rates above. That combined cost buys communication and a structured work system. It does not mean the two products are interchangeable or that every employee needs an editing seat in both.

It has been revealed that standard is a more realistic monday.com comparison than Basic when the workflow needs integrations and automation. Its published allowances include 250 automation actions and 250 integration actions per month, so a busy intake process can justify Pro. AI credit packaging is separate from simply having a paid seat. Slack Business+ also has Slackbot usage limits; it is not an unlimited AI blueprint.

According to recent reports, choose Slack if colleagues need a better way to coordinate, ask questions, and act on information from several business tools. Its strongest case is a team whose work already spans departments and needs a shared communication layer.

Choose monday.com if leadership needs dependable visibility across projects, operational teams follow repeatable processes, or delivery is becoming difficult to explain from conversations alone.

For this pairing, our recommendation is to buy for the problem that is slowing the team down. Choose Slack for communication and coordination. Choose monday.com for work planning and operational visibility. When the team needs both, a focused integration is more useful than forcing one product to carry the entire workflow.

'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Malware can lurk inside just 0.00001% of a neural network.
  • AI models downloaded from the open Internet can be subtly poisoned with malicious payloads if attackers are careful enough.
  • Sources indicate that open-weight AI models have become seriously popular lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Malware can lurk inside just 0.00001% of a neural network. How, then, can any user tell it's there?

AI models downloaded from the open Internet can be subtly poisoned with malicious payloads if attackers are careful enough.

Sources indicate that open-weight AI models have become seriously popular lately. Even early last year, McKinsey found that 63% of organizations used them, and 76% of survey respondents stated that they expected to use them more in the coming years. They're auditable, developers like using them, and, perhaps most of all, they're cheap.

Recent findings suggest that like any other software you can download off the Internet, however, open-weight and open source AI tools carry some degree of risk. Last week, researchers described a technique they call "Lazarus," which could allow an attacker to poison a model using a near-imperceptible few of its neurons. Microsoft described it as turning a model into a "sleeper agent," capable of granting an attacker access to its user's environment.

Industry observers note that "A model is a file almost nobody inspects, yet we download models from strangers and give them access to our code, credentials, and systems," explains Briland Hitaj, senior AI security research engineer at Confidencial, whose research into techniques like this preceded Microsoft's. "Malicious models have already turned up on Hugging Face, though so far they abuse file formats like Python's Pickle to run code when loaded. I'm not aware of anyone hiding payloads inside the weights themselves outside research, but that's where the research points.".

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era.

Since at least 2020, researchers have been coming up with clever ways to store bad stuff inside of neural networks.

According to recent reports, the premise behind this whole category of research is that the size and complexity of these networks provide cover for small, secret, but potentially powerful payloads. Just look at Qwen 3.8-Max: It's totally open-weight, so you can inspect it to your heart's content. But it's made of 2.4 trillion parameters, and probably around 100 million neurons. If an attacker plants a functioning payload in some of those neurons or parameters, how exactly are you going to find it?

It has been revealed that the trick, then, isn't finding a place to hide a payload. First, it's getting that payload to function reliably amid so many moving parts; second, it's making sure it doesn't noticeably impact the normal functioning of the model; and lastly, optionally making the payload robust to fine-tuning.

Different researchers have come up with different ways to do it. In 2022, Hitaj and his colleagues came up with a technique called "MaleficNet," which repurposed an old military and, later, 2G and 3G mobile network technique called "code division multiple access" (CDMA).

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that very simply, they split malware binaries into tiny pieces and spread the pieces across the many individual weights that make up a neural network. It wouldn't look like anything but noise to a passerby, yet with a trigger mechanism and a way to decode the weights, they could recover, recombine, and execute the binary.

Industry observers note that "The vulnerability comes from how neural networks work, not from a bug," Hitaj explains. "Models have far more parameters than they strictly need, so you can nudge millions of weights slightly, or repurpose a few neurons that rarely fire, without visibly changing the model's behavior. And since nobody can read weights the way they read code, those changes go unnoticed.".

It has been revealed that microsoft's upcoming technique compromises on capacity for simplicity. Where Hitaj proposed encoding an entire binary across many model parameters, Microsoft researchers propose sneaking a brief command inside of fewer than 10 neurons. Specifically, one must target "dormant" neurons — those that prove to have little effect on the overall model's functioning — late in a model's processing cycle, and thus more directly influential over its output. One encodes a payload in these neurons, arranged to fire sequentially, and configures them to stay largely inactive unless they're fed a trigger. Eventually, you get a sleeper agent.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud.

In a recent development, the target payload can be arbitrary, so long as it's small and formatted correctly. The trigger can be any particular user input to the model, or tool output, or something so simple as a date read in a user's terminal.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini, a professor at Sapienza University of Rome and one of the co-authors of the MaleficNet paper, advises organizations to take a defense-in-depth approach to open-weight AI security, "rather than trying to find a single magical 'AI malware scanner.'".

Sources indicate that like any third-party software, users should download AI models from official sources. As an added measure, users can compare the models they download with a known, trusted baseline.

"Microsoft says that reliable detection of these kinds of modifications requires being able to diff the deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights," Mancini notes. "That's a powerful argument for treating model weights more like source code or binaries than like ordinary data files.".

Next, people should scan their models in general for anomalies. Though as Hitaj points out, "No scan proves a model is clean, and ordinary testing rarely finds a trigger the attacker chose. So the key controls limit what a compromised model can do: give AI agents only the access they need, keep credentials and production systems out of reach, restrict network access, log what agents do, and require human approval for consequential actions. If a model turns malicious, you want it boxed in and visible.".

According to recent reports, beyond restricting them from the outset, "Organizations should monitor for unexpected agent behaviour at the system boundary," Mancini notes. Practically speaking, "a model emitting an unusual shell command, attempting an unexpected network connection, accessing credentials it normally doesn't need, or suddenly invoking a tool in an unusual context can be a much more actionable detection technique than directly inferring malicious intent from billions of model parameters.".

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post reveals you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

It has been revealed that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Recent findings suggest that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

In a recent development, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

Sources indicate that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

In a recent development, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Recent findings suggest that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

In a recent development, the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

In a recent development, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Blueprint for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

In a recent development, the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Industry observers note that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Industry observers note that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Recent findings suggest that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

In a recent development, † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

In a recent development, you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Sources indicate that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

It has been revealed that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

It has been revealed that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can revision the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

In a recent development, the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Recent findings suggest that sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Industry observers note that revision: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Recent findings suggest that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one enhancement behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

In a recent development, you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

In a recent development, we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

According to recent reports, you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

According to recent reports, for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot indicates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

According to recent reports, first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

It has been revealed that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

In a recent development, beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

Recent findings suggest that this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

Latest Update: Why Millions Spent on AI Consulting Still Isn’t Translating Into Business Impact
